Your biggest bottleneck is your storage. The rest would work fine with any distro and desktop environment. Here's your options:
1. Get an SSD and install any Linux distro you want.
2. Keep using the HDD, but be picky to install smaller and simpler distros to avoid your OS having to read from disk too much.

Option 2 splits off into 2 sub-options:
2.1. Limit yourself to distros with very lightweight DEs or WMs.
Stuff like Q4OS with Trinity, MX Linux with Fluxbox, Fedora with Sway, antiX with IceWM/Fluxbox, etc. The lighter/simpler a DE is and the less background services it has, the less busy your HDD will be and the snappier things will feel. Fluxbox, Openbox and Sway specifically are often used in cheap Chinese Linux handhelds that run the OS from a microSD card and have 500MB-2GB of RAM.
Slightly heavier but more usable options would be Q4OS with KDE and MX Linux with Xfce.
2.2. Install an older distro that is still supported.
Ubuntu 16/18/20 LTS and Debian 11 are still supported for a few more years. Older software has less code and features, so you'll save system resources that way. You'll still get security updates with these.

It does. Opening stuff is much faster on an SSD. It's the difference between your system settings opening in 0.5-2 seconds on an SSD vs 2-8 seconds on an HDD. Also since you have a low amount of RAM your OS won't cache things into memory as often, so re-opening your settings will take a while too.
Now imagine this difference across hundreds of your system files and services that are used daily.

I would personally rather use an ultra-light distro that runs fully in-memory (Porteus, Puppy, antiX, etc.), no matter how minimal/barebones it is, than have to go back to using HDDs (especially ones that old).
